Emergence of Chaos

SequencesAlgebraLimits
Game: This shows what happens when a number is fed back into the same rule again and again: sometimes it settles, sometimes it loops, sometimes it wanders.
How to play: Drag the slider or tap the right-hand picture to pick the number a. Press "New starting point" to send the dot off again; the arrow keys work on the picture too.
The rule, drawn as a web Where the dots end up, for each a
Look for the math

Nothing on this page is random once you have chosen a and the starting number x. The very same rule is followed at every step, yet for some values of a the result looks completely unpredictable. That is the surprise called chaos: random-looking behaviour with a perfectly deterministic cause.

A rule that eats its own answer

The rule is the logistic map, written here with k = 4a so that the highest point of its graph is always exactly a (put x = 1/2 and you get 4a · 1/2 · 1/2 = a):

xn+1 = f(xn) = 4a xn (1 − xn)

The iteration is drawn on the left as a cobweb: go straight up to the curve, then sideways to the diagonal y = x, and do it again. Starting near zero, the first steps move away from zero, because the slope there is 4a > 1.

One resting spot becomes two

A fixed point solves x = f(x). Besides x = 0 there is x = 1 − 1/(4a). Its slope is f′(x) = 2 − 4a, so it attracts while |2 − 4a| < 1. At a = 0.75 that size is exactly 1 — the spot stops attracting, and the dot begins to alternate between two places. The two spots remain attractive until a = (1 + √6)/4 = 0.86237..., the page's 0.86237 threshold, which our logic test confirms.

Doublings, faster and faster

After that the two spots become four, then eight, then sixteen. The bifurcation diagram on the right shows each of these splits: one strand turns into two, two into four, and the gaps between splits get smaller each time. They pile up at a ≈ 0.8925 — the page says "a = .892", which is right to three decimal places — and beyond it the dot races around the whole interval. Our test checks the periods 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 directly by iterating the rule.

Windows of order, and what the applet actually draws

Order returns in small windows even after the cascade: near a = 0.957 there is a three-step cycle, which then doubles to six, twelve and twenty-four; the test finds all four. At a = 0.8, the graph of f(f(x)) crosses the diagonal in four places: zero (a repeller), the old fixed point (a repeller), and the two spots of the attractive two-cycle. In general a spot is attractive when |f′(x)| < 1 and repelling when it is greater than 1.

One honest caveat: the original applet draws only 4, 8 or 24 points per column below a = 0.872, then height/4 or height/2 above it, and throws away round(100/a + 20) starting values. Those are drawing choices, not facts about the map; we kept them so the right-hand picture looks the same. The page itself notes that twenty-four steps are about all the old program can resolve, and our double-precision version agrees.

Try moving the slider slowly from 0.86 to 0.90 and watch one strand of the right-hand picture split into two, then four, then eight.
